The Weight of Unsent Messages

I have a folder on my phone. It's called "Drafts" but it's really a graveyard. Forty-seven messages I started and abandoned. Some are to people I love. Some are to people I used to love. A few are to people I don't even like anymore, which is its own kind of mystery.

There's one to my mother that begins "I know you don't understand why I—" and stops there. I wrote it three years ago. I've written versions of it since. The sentence keeps wanting to finish itself differently each time, which tells me something, though I'm not sure what.

The thing about unsent messages is that they feel like they exist in a different tense. Not past, not future. Some kind of suspended present where the words are still floating, still possible, still *yours* alone. Once you send them, they belong to the other person. They become evidence. They can be screenshotted, misread, held against you in arguments you didn't know you were having.

I think about this too much. I think about how my grandmother never sent a text message in her life. She wrote letters, actual letters, with stamps and envelopes and the physical weight of paper. She kept them in a box. When she died, we found hundreds. She had written to people who were already dead, sometimes. She didn't care. The writing was the point.

My grandfather, her husband, kept a notebook. Not a journal—he hated that word, too self-conscious. Just a notebook where he wrote down things he noticed. "The way light hits the kitchen floor at 4pm in October." "Mrs. Patterson's cat, the orange one, finally caught a bird." Small observations, accumulated over forty years. When he died, we read them. It was like getting to know him again, but slower. More carefully.

I don't know what will happen to my drafts folder. Probably nothing. It'll get backed up to some cloud server, then forgotten, then eventually deleted by some automated process I won't understand. The messages will disappear without ever having been read by their intended recipients. Is that better or worse than sending them? I genuinely don't know.

There's a message to an ex that I've rewritten eleven times. It's about forgiveness, or maybe it's about blame. The lines blur. I wanted to say something true, but I also wanted to be understood, and those are different projects. Maybe they're incompatible. Maybe that's why I never sent it. Maybe I was protecting myself, or maybe I was protecting the version of her that exists in my head, the one who might read it and feel something, and then the real her would be disappointed by whatever I actually wrote.

I sent a message last week. It was simple. "Thinking of you." She wrote back an hour later. We talked for a while. It was good. It was also, I realized afterward, a kind of performance. We were both performing being okay, being connected, being people who had moved on. The message itself was fine. The context around it was a construction. We build these little theaters for each other, don't we? Small stages where we can be the people we wish we were.

My therapist says I intellectualize my feelings. I think she's right. I think I do it because feelings are heavy and words are light, and I like things I can hold up to the light and examine from different angles. But feelings don't work that way. They just sit there, in your chest, making it hard to breathe sometimes. You can't examine them. You can only carry them, or put them down, or let someone else help you carry them.

I'm trying to put some down. That's what this is, I guess. Practice. Writing without an audience, or with an audience of one who will never read it. The page doesn't judge. The page doesn't need anything from me. It just receives.

There's a message in my drafts to a friend who moved to another country. I started it the day she left. "I don't know how to—" and then nothing. I've tried to write it again so many times. But the not-knowing was the point, wasn't it? The not-knowing how to be her friend from far away. The not-knowing how to miss someone without making them feel guilty for leaving. The not-knowing how to want things for other people that they don't want for themselves.

She texts me sometimes. Short messages. "Saw a dog that looked like yours." "Ate something spicy and thought of you." We've built a language of small things. It's not the same as what we had. But it's something. It's a bridge, maybe, or a rope, or just a habit we're maintaining because stopping feels like admitting something.

I used to think that honesty was the highest virtue in relationships. Now I think it's more complicated. Sometimes honesty is a gift. Sometimes it's a weapon. Sometimes it's just noise, the sound of your own voice echoing in a room where no one asked you to speak. The drafts folder is where I put the honesty I'm not sure about. The honesty that might hurt. The honesty that might be misunderstood. The honesty that I'm not even sure is true, because feelings change, and by the time I finish a sentence, I might feel differently than when I started it.

There's a message to myself. I write these sometimes, when I can't sleep. "You are not behind." "You are not failing." "The thing you're afraid of is not as likely as you think." They don't work, not really. But they're something to do with my hands, with my mind, when the dark is too quiet and my thoughts start circling. The drafts folder holds these too. A conversation with myself that never quite ends.

I wonder if everyone has this. The hidden archive of almost-said things. The words that got caught in the throat. The love that was too big for its container and spilled over, leaving stains. I think we do. I think we carry these ghosts around, these unborn messages, and they shape us in ways we don't acknowledge. They make us more careful, or less careful. They make us brave in some areas and cowardly in others. They are, in their way, a kind of autobiography. The story of who we almost were, who we almost said we were, to the people who mattered.

I'm going to delete some of them. Not all. Some I want to keep, as evidence. As proof that I felt these things, intensely, even if I never expressed them properly. The rest—I'll let them go. They've served their purpose. They've been witnesses. Now they can be released.

Or maybe I'll keep them. Maybe I'll back them up, encrypt them, hide them somewhere only I can find. A time capsule of my almosts. For whoever I become, someday, to discover. To understand. To forgive, maybe, or to finally understand what I was afraid of.

The cursor blinks. Waiting. I could write more. I probably will, eventually. There's always more. There's always the next thing to almost say, the next feeling to almost name, the next love to almost give away.

But for now, I'll stop here. I'll leave this unsent, too. A message to no one, about the difficulty of messages, about the weight of words we carry and the words we release. About the strange mercy of the drafts folder, where nothing is final, where everything is still possible, where we can be brave and cowardly at the same time, where we can practice being the people we're trying to become.

Goodnight, drafts folder. Goodnight, almosts. Goodnight, all of us, writing in the dark, hoping someone will someday read what we couldn't send.
